Chen et al., ``Straggler mitigation in edge computing via adaptive regularization,'' in \\textit{IEEE TPDS}, 2024.\n\\end{thebibliography}\n\n\\end{document}\n\n## Naprawa Thesis.md: Weryfikacja Hypergraphu i Koncepcja Adaptive FedProx\n\\documentclass[conference]{IEEEtran}\n\\usepackage{cite}\n\\usepackage{amsmath,amssymb,amsfonts}\n\\usepackage{algorithmic}\n\\usepackage{graphicx}\n\\usepackage{textcomp}\n\\usepackage{xcolor}\n\\usepackage{tikz}\n\\usetikzlibrary{shapes,arrows,calc,positioning,fit}\n\n\\begin{document}\n\n\\title{Adaptive FedProx: Mitigating Straggler Impact in Non-IID Federated Learning via Proximal Optimization}\n\n\\author{\\IEEEauthorblockN{Author Name}\\IEEEauthorblockA{Department of Computer Science, Institution Name\\\\City, Country\\\\email@domain.com}}\n\n\\maketitle\n\n\\begin{abstract}\nFederated Learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across distributed edge devices while preserving data privacy. However, its performance degrades significantly under non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data conditions and the presence of \\textit{stragglers}—slow or offline clients that bottleneck global aggregation. This paper investigates the interaction between static proximal regularization parameters ($\\mu$) and heterogeneous client dynamics in Adaptive FedProx. We introduce a modified proximal optimization module that dynamically adjusts the regularization strength to counteract gradient divergence caused by non-IID distributions (modeled via Dirichlet partitions with $\\alpha = 0.5$) and partial client dropout. Experimental results on a simulated cluster of 10 clients demonstrate that our approach reduces the \\textit{divergence rate} compared to baseline FedAvg while maintaining high accuracy under 25\\% straggler rates.\n\\end{abstract}\n\n\\begin{IEEEkeywords}\nFederated Learning, Proximal Optimization, Non-IID Data, Stragglers, Adaptive Regularization, Edge Computing\n\\end{IEEEkeywords}\n\n\\section{Introduction \\& Problem Formulation}\\label{sec:intro}\nThe proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has shifted machine learning workloads to the edge. Federated Averaging (FedAvg) \\cite{mcmahan2017communication} remains the standard protocol, allowing clients to train locally and share updates with a central server. However, two critical challenges undermine its efficacy:\n\n\\subsection{Motivation: Heterogeneity and Stragglers}\nFirst, non-IID data distributions cause significant \\textit{client drift}. When data is partitioned using a Dirichlet distribution with low concentration $\\alpha$ (e.g., \\ref_ast{config.py:DIRICHLET_ALPHA}), local gradients diverge from the global gradient direction. Second, network instability leads to \\textit{stragglers}. In environments described in \\cite{kairouz2024advances}, waiting for all $K$ clients to complete computation introduces unacceptable latency. Ignoring slow clients (partial participation) can further skew the model if not handled correctly.\n\n\\subsection{Thesis Statement}\nThis paper posits that dynamically adapting the proximal parameter $\\mu$, based on the static baseline \\ref_ast{config.py:MU_PROXIMAL}, mitigates divergence in non-IID settings without increasing communication overhead. We hypothesize that \\textbf{Adaptive FedProx} achieves a superior balance between \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:final_accuracy} and \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:straggler_resilience_rate} compared to static regularization.\n\n\\section{Related Work and SOTA Taxonomy}\\label{sec:sota}\nEarly FL frameworks relied on simple averaging. To address client drift, FedProx \\cite{li2020federated} introduced a proximal penalty term $(\\mu/2)\\|w - w^t\\|^2$. While effective for homogeneous IIDs, static $\\mu$ fails to adapt to varying local gradient norms in non-IID scenarios \\cite{wang2023tackling}. \n\nRecent works (2023--2024) have explored adaptive strategies. Karimireddy et al. \\cite{karimireddy2024scaffold} utilized control variates to correct drift but at high communication cost. Other approaches like FedNova \\cite{wang2020fednova} normalize updates by local epochs, addressing the bias introduced by varying computation times. Our work synthesizes these insights by focusing on the proximal parameter's adaptability under straggler constraints.\n\n\\section{System Architecture and Mathematical Formalism}\\label{sec:architecture}\nThe proposed system consists of a central server and $N$ client devices (defined as \\ref_ast{config.py:NUM_CLIENTS}). The data partitioning follows a Dirichlet distribution $P_{kn} \\sim \\text{Dir}(\\alpha)$, ensuring non-IID characteristics.\n\n\\subsection{Adaptive Proximal Loss}\nThe local objective for client $k$ at round $t$ is:\n\\begin{equation}\n    L_k(w; w^t) = f_k(w) + \\frac{\\mu_{dynamic}}{2} \\|w - w^t\\|^2\n\\end{equation}\nwhere $\\mu_{dynamic}$ is adjusted based on the local gradient norm to The data partitioning follows a Dirichlet distribution $P_{kn} \\sim \\text{Dir}(\\alpha)$, ensuring non-IID characteristics.\n\n### A. Adaptive Proximal Loss\nThe local objective for client $k$ at round $t$ is:\n\\begin{equation}\n    L_k(w; w^t) = f_k(w) + \\frac{\\mu_{dynamic}}{2} \\|w - w^t\\|^2\n\\end{equation}\nwhere $\\mu_{dynamic}$ is adjusted based on the local gradient norm to stabilize convergence. This dynamic adjustment addresses the limitations of static proximal parameters (e.g., \\ref_ast{config.py:MU_PROXIMAL}) in heterogeneous environments.\n\n### B. Distributed Architecture Diagram\nFigure \\ref{fig:architecture} illustrates the data flow and aggregation logic, including straggler handling mechanisms.\n\n\\begin{figure}[t]\n    \\centering\n fill=green!10] {Client $K$: SGD\\n($\\mu_{dyn}$)};\n        \\node (dropout) [draw, rectangle, below of=clientN, yshift=-1.2cm, xshift=1.5cm, minimum width=2cm, minimum height=0.5cm, fill=red!10, Handling.}\n    \\label{fig:architecture}\n\\end{figure}\n\n## Section IV: Implementation Details & Experimental Setup\n\nOur simulation environment is implemented in Python, utilizing a custom core module for federated aggregation. Key hyperparameters are centralized in \\ref_ast{config.py}. We simulate $N=10$ clients with $L=\\ref_ast{config.py:LOCAL_EPOCHS}$ local epochs and learning rate \\ref_ast{config.py:LEARNING_RATE}. Data is split using the function `generate_federated_partitions` from \\ref_ast{core.py}, applying a Dirichlet prior of $\\alpha=0.5$. The training loop runs for \\ref_ast{config.py:ROUNDS} rounds.\n\n## Section V: Empirical Results & Ablation Study\n\nWe evaluate the proposed Adaptive FedProx against standard FedAvg and static FedProx over \\ref_ast{config.py:ROUNDS} communication rounds. The simulation introduces a 25% straggler rate by randomly dropping client updates in each round.\n\n### A. Convergence and Accuracy\nAs shown in Figure \\ref{fig:comparison}, our proposed method achieves a final accuracy of \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:final_accuracy}, outperforming the baseline FedAvg (\\ref_csv{results.csv:baseline:final_accuracy}). Chen et al., ``Straggler mitigation in edge computing via adaptive regularization,'' in \\textit{IEEE TPDS}, 2024.\n\\end{thebibliography}\n\n\\end{document}\n\n## Naprawa Thesis.md: Weryfikacja Hypergraphu i Koncepcja Adaptive FedProx\n\\documentclass[conference]{IEEEtran}\n\\usepackage{cite}\n\\usepackage{amsmath,amssymb,amsfonts}\n\\usepackage{algorithmic}\n\\usepackage{graphicx}\n\\usepackage{textcomp}\n\\usepackage{xcolor}\n\\usepackage{tikz}\n\\usetikzlibrary{shapes,arrows,calc,positioning,fit}\n\n\\begin{document}\n\n\\title{Adaptive FedProx: Mitigating Straggler Impact in Non-IID Federated Learning via Proximal Optimization}\n\n\\author{\\IEEEauthorblockN{Author Name}\\IEEEauthorblockA{Department of Computer Science, Institution Name\\\\City, Country\\\\email@domain.com}}\n\n\\maketitle\n\n\\begin{abstract}\nFederated Learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across distributed edge devices while preserving data privacy. However, its performance degrades significantly under non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data conditions and the presence of \\textit{stragglers}—slow or offline clients that bottleneck global aggregation. This paper investigates the interaction between static proximal regularization parameters ($\\mu$) and heterogeneous client dynamics in Adaptive FedProx. We introduce a modified proximal optimization module that dynamically adjusts the regularization strength to counteract gradient divergence caused by non-IID distributions (modeled via Dirichlet partitions with $\\alpha = 0.5$) and partial client dropout. Experimental results on a simulated cluster of 10 clients demonstrate that our approach reduces the \\textit{divergence rate} compared to baseline FedAvg while maintaining high accuracy under 25\\% straggler rates.\n\\end{abstract}\n\n\\begin{IEEEkeywords}\nFederated Learning, Proximal Optimization, Non-IID Data, Stragglers, Adaptive Regularization, Edge Computing\n\\end{IEEEkeywords}\n\n\\section{Introduction \\& Problem Formulation}\\label{sec:intro}\nThe proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has shifted machine learning workloads to the edge. Federated Averaging (FedAvg) \\cite{mcmahan2017communication} remains the standard protocol, allowing clients to train locally and share updates with a central server. However, two critical challenges undermine its efficacy:\n\n\\subsection{Motivation: Heterogeneity and Stragglers}\nFirst, non-IID data distributions cause significant \\textit{client drift}. When data is partitioned using a Dirichlet distribution with low concentration $\\alpha$ (e.g., \\ref_ast{config.py:DIRICHLET_ALPHA}), local gradients diverge from the global gradient direction. Second, network instability leads to \\textit{stragglers}. In environments described in \\cite{kairouz2024advances}, waiting for all $K$ clients to complete computation introduces unacceptable latency. Ignoring slow clients (partial participation) can further skew the model if not handled correctly.\n\n\\subsection{Thesis Statement}\nThis paper posits that dynamically adapting the proximal parameter $\\mu$, based on the static baseline \\ref_ast{config.py:MU_PROXIMAL}, mitigates divergence in non-IID settings without increasing communication overhead. We hypothesize that \\textbf{Adaptive FedProx} achieves a superior balance between \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:final_accuracy} and \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:straggler_resilience_rate} compared to static regularization.\n\n\\section{Related Work and SOTA Taxonomy}\\label{sec:sota}\nEarly FL frameworks relied on simple averaging. To address client drift, FedProx \\cite{li2020federated} introduced a proximal penalty term $(\\mu/2)\\|w - w^t\\|^2$. While effective for homogeneous IIDs, static $\\mu$ fails to adapt to varying local gradient norms in non-IID scenarios \\cite{wang2023tackling}. \n\nRecent works (2023--2024) have explored adaptive strategies. Karimireddy et al. \\cite{karimireddy2024scaffold} utilized control variates to correct drift but at high communication cost. Other approaches like FedNova \\cite{wang2020fednova} normalize updates by local epochs, addressing the bias introduced by varying computation times. Our work synthesizes these insights by focusing on the proximal parameter's adaptability under straggler constraints.\n\n\\section{System Architecture and Mathematical Formalism}\\label{sec:architecture}\nThe proposed system consists of a central server and $N$ client devices (defined as \\ref_ast{config.py:NUM_CLIENTS}). The data partitioning follows a Dirichlet distribution $P_{kn} \\sim \\text{Dir}(\\alpha)$, ensuring non-IID characteristics.\n\n\\subsection{Adaptive Proximal Loss}\nThe local objective for client $k$ at round $t$ is:\n\\begin{equation}\n    L_k(w; w^t) = f_k(w) + \\frac{\\mu_{dynamic}}{2} \\|w - w^t\\|^2\n\\end{equation}\nwhere $\\mu_{dynamic}$ is adjusted based on the local gradient norm to stabilize convergence.\n\n\\subsection{Distributed Architecture Diagram}\\label{ssec:arch_diagram}\nFigure \\ref{fig:architecture} illustrates the data flow and aggregation The simulation introduces a 25\\% straggler rate by randomly dropping client updates in each round.\n\n\\subsection{Convergence and Accuracy}\nAs shown in Figure \\ref{fig:comparison}, our proposed method achieves a final accuracy of \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:final_accuracy}, outperforming the baseline FedAvg (\\ref_csv{results.csv:baseline:final_accuracy}). As detailed in \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:straggler_resilience_rate}, the proposed method maintains higher model stability compared to static baselines when handling dropped updates.\n\n\\begin{figure}[t]\n    \\centering\n    \\includegraphics[width=\\columnwidth, keepaspectratio]{figures/comparison_chart.pdf}\n    \\caption{Convergence and Straggler Comparison Charts. Left: Accuracy over Rounds. Right: Resilience Metrics.}\n    \\label{fig:comparison}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\section{Conclusion}\\label{sec:conclusion}\nThis paper presented an Adaptive FedProx module that addresses the dual challenges of non-IID data and straggler clients in federated learning. Chen et al., ``Straggler mitigation in edge computing via adaptive regularization,'' in \\textit{IEEE TPDS}, 2024.\n\\end{thebibliography}\n\n\\end{document}\n\n## Naprawa Thesis.md: Weryfikacja Hypergraphu i Koncepcja Adaptive FedProx\n\\documentclass[conference]{IEEEtran}\n\\usepackage{cite}\n\\usepackage{amsmath,amssymb,amsfonts}\n\\usepackage{algorithmic}\n\\usepackage{graphicx}\n\\usepackage{textcomp}\n\\usepackage{xcolor}\n\\usepackage{tikz}\n\\usetikzlibrary{shapes,arrows,calc,positioning,fit}\n\n\\begin{document}\n\n\\title{Adaptive FedProx: Mitigating Straggler Impact in Non-IID Federated Learning via Proximal Optimization}\n\n\\author{\\IEEEauthorblockN{Author Name}\\IEEEauthorblockA{Department of Computer Science, Institution Name\\\\City, Country\\\\email@domain.com}}\n\n\\maketitle\n\n\\begin{abstract}\nFederated Learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across distributed edge devices while preserving data privacy. However, its performance degrades significantly under non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data conditions and the presence of \\textit{stragglers}—slow or offline clients that bottleneck global aggregation. This paper investigates the interaction between static proximal regularization parameters ($\\mu$) and heterogeneous client dynamics in Adaptive FedProx. We introduce a modified proximal optimization module that dynamically adjusts the regularization strength to counteract gradient divergence caused by non-IID distributions (modeled via Dirichlet partitions with $\\alpha = 0.5$) and partial client dropout. Experimental results on a simulated cluster of 10 clients demonstrate that our approach reduces the \\textit{divergence rate} compared to baseline FedAvg while maintaining high accuracy under 25\\% straggler rates.\n\\end{abstract}\n\n\\begin{IEEEkeywords}\nFederated Learning, Proximal Optimization, Non-IID Data, Stragglers, Adaptive Regularization, Edge Computing\n\\end{IEEEkeywords}\n\n\\section{Introduction \\& Problem Formulation}\\label{sec:intro}\nThe proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has shifted machine learning workloads to the edge. Federated Averaging (FedAvg) \\cite{mcmahan2017communication} remains the standard protocol, allowing clients to train locally and share updates with a central server. However, two critical challenges undermine its efficacy:\n\n\\subsection{Motivation: Heterogeneity and Stragglers}\nFirst, non-IID data distributions cause significant \\textit{client drift}. When data is partitioned using a Dirichlet distribution with low concentration $\\alpha$ (e.g., \\ref_ast{config.py:DIRICHLET_ALPHA}), local gradients diverge from the global gradient direction. Second, network instability leads to \\textit{stragglers}. In environments described in \\cite{kairouz2024advances}, waiting for all $K$ clients to complete computation introduces unacceptable latency. Ignoring slow clients (partial participation) can further skew the model if not handled correctly.\n\n\\subsection{Thesis Statement}\nThis paper posits that dynamically adapting the proximal parameter $\\mu$, based on the static baseline \\ref_ast{config.py:MU_PROXIMAL}, mitigates divergence in non-IID settings without increasing communication overhead. We hypothesize that \\textbf{Adaptive FedProx} achieves a superior balance between \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:final_accuracy} and \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:straggler_resilience_rate} compared to static regularization.\n\n\\section{Related Work and SOTA Taxonomy}\\label{sec:sota}\nEarly FL frameworks relied on simple averaging. To address client drift, FedProx \\cite{li2020federated} introduced a proximal penalty term $(\\mu/2)\\|w - w^t\\|^2$. While effective for homogeneous IIDs, static $\\mu$ fails to adapt to varying local gradient norms in non-IID scenarios \\cite{wang2023tackling}. \n\nRecent works (2023--2024) have explored adaptive strategies. Karimireddy et al. \\cite{karimireddy2024scaffold} utilized control variates to correct drift but at high communication cost. Other approaches like FedNova \\cite{wang2020fednova} normalize updates by local epochs, addressing the bias introduced by varying computation times. Our work synthesizes these insights by focusing on the proximal parameter's adaptability under straggler constraints.\n\n\\section{System Architecture and Mathematical Formalism}\\label{sec:architecture}\nThe proposed system consists of a central server and $N$ client devices (defined as \\ref_ast{config.py:NUM_CLIENTS}). The data partitioning follows a Dirichlet distribution $P_{kn} \\sim \\text{Dir}(\\alpha)$, ensuring non-IID characteristics.\n\n\\subsection{Adaptive Proximal Loss}\nThe local objective for client $k$ at round $t$ is:\n\\begin{equation}\n    L_k(w; w^t) = f_k(w) + \\frac{\\mu_{dynamic}}{2} \\|w - w^t\\|^2\n\\end{equation}\nwhere $\\mu_{dynamic}$ is adjusted based on the local gradient norm to stabilize convergence.\n\n\\subsection{Distributed Architecture Diagram}\\label{ssec:arch_diagram}\nFigure \\ref{fig:architecture} illustrates the data flow and aggregation Details}\\label{sec:implementation}\nOur simulation environment is implemented in Python, utilizing a custom core module for federated aggregation. Key hyperparameters are centralized in \\ref_ast{config.py}. We simulate $N=10$ clients with $L=\\ref_ast{config.py:LOCAL_EPOCHS}$ local epochs and learning rate \\ref_ast{config.py:LEARNING_RATE}. Data is split using the function \\texttt{generate_federated_partitions} from \\ref_ast{core.py}, applying a Dirichlet prior of $\\alpha=0.5$.\n\n\\section{Empirical Results}\\label{sec:results}\nWe evaluate the proposed Adaptive FedProx against standard FedAvg and static FedProx over \\ref_ast{config.py:ROUNDS} communication rounds. The simulation introduces a 25\\% straggler rate by randomly dropping client updates in each round.\n\n\\subsection{Convergence and Accuracy}\nAs shown in Figure \\ref{fig:comparison}, our proposed method achieves a final accuracy of \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:final_accuracy}, outperforming the baseline FedAvg (\\ref_csv{results.csv:baseline:final_accuracy}). The adaptive mechanism successfully reduces the divergence rate caused by non-IID gradients.\n\n\\subsection{Straggler Resilience}\nThe system demonstrates robustness to partial participation. As detailed in \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:straggler_resilience_rate}, the proposed method maintains higher model stability compared to static baselines when handling dropped updates.\n\n\\begin{figure}[t]\n    \\centering\n    \\includegraphics[width=\\columnwidth, keepaspectratio]{figures/comparison_chart.pdf}\n    \\caption{Convergence and Straggler Comparison Charts. Left: Accuracy over Rounds. Right: Resilience Metrics.}\n    \\label{fig:comparison}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\section{Conclusion}\\label{sec:conclusion}\nThis paper presented an Adaptive FedProx module that addresses the dual challenges of non-IID data and straggler clients in federated learning. The data partitioning follows a Dirichlet distribution $P_{kn} \\sim \\text{Dir}(\\alpha)$, ensuring non-IID characteristics.\n\n\\subsection{Adaptive Proximal Loss}\nThe local objective for client $k$ at round $t$ is:\n\\begin{equation}\n    L_k(w; w^t) = f_k(w) + \\frac{\\mu_{dynamic}}{2} \\|w - w^t\\|^2\n\\end{equation}\nwhere $\\mu_{dynamic}$ is adjusted based on the local gradient norm to stabilize convergence. This dynamic adjustment addresses the limitations of static proximal parameters (e.g., \\ref_ast{config.py:MU_PROXIMAL}) in heterogeneous environments.\n\n\\subsection{Distributed Architecture Diagram}\\label{ssec:arch_diagram}\nFigure \\ref{fig:architecture} illustrates the data flow and aggregation logic, including straggler handling mechanisms.\n\n\\begin{figure}[t]\n    \\centering\n    \\resizebox{0.95\\columnwidth}{!}{%\n    \\begin{tikzpicture}[node distance=1.2cm, auto]\n        % Nodes\n        \\node (server) [draw, rectangle, minimum width=4cm, minimum height=1cm, height=0.8cm, fill=green!10] {Client 1: Local SGD\\n($\\mu_{dyn}$)};\n        \\node (client2) [draw, rectangle, below of=server, yshift=-2.5cm, xshift=0cm, minimum width=3.5cm, minimum height=0.8cm, fill=green!10] {Client $k$: Local SGD\\n($\\mu_{dyn}$)};\n        \\node (clientN) [draw, rectangle, below of=server, yshift=-2.5cm, xshift=3cm, minimum width=3.5cm, minimum height=0.8cm, fill=green!10] {Client $K$: Local SGD\\n($\\mu_{dyn}$)};\n        \\node (dropout) [draw, rectangle, below of=clientN, yshift=-1.5cm, xshift=1.5cm, minimum width=2cm, minimum height=0.6cm, fill=red!10, dashed] {Straggler\\n(Dropped)};\n        % Arrows\n        \\draw[->, thick] (server) -- node[left] {Global $w^t$} (client1);\n        \\draw[->, thick] (server) -- node[right] {Global $w^t$} (client2);\n        \\draw[->, thick] (server) -- node[right] {Global $w^t$} (clientN);\n        \\draw[->, thick] (client1) -- node[left] {$\\Delta w_1$} (server);\n        \\draw[->, thick] (client2) -- node[right] {$\\Delta w_k$} (server);\n        \\draw[->, thick, dashed, red] (clientN) -- node[right] {Timeout} (dropout);\n    \\end{tikzpicture}%}\n    \\caption{Distributed Adaptive FedProx Architecture with Straggler Handling.}\n    \\label{fig:architecture}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\section{Implementation Details}\\label{sec:implementation}\nOur simulation environment is implemented in Python, utilizing a custom core module for federated aggregation. Key hyperparameters are centralized in \\ref_ast{config.py}. We simulate $N=10$ clients with $L=\\ref_ast{config.py:LOCAL_EPOCHS}$ local epochs and learning rate \\ref_ast{config.py:LEARNING_RATE}. Data is split using the function \\texttt{generate_federated_partitions} from \\ref_ast{core.py}, applying a Dirichlet prior of $\\alpha=0.5$.\n\n\\section{Empirical Results}\\label{sec:results}\nWe evaluate the proposed Adaptive FedProx against standard FedAvg and static FedProx over \\ref_ast{config.py:ROUNDS} communication rounds. The simulation introduces a 25\\% straggler rate by randomly dropping client updates in each round.\n\n\\subsection{Convergence and Accuracy}\nAs shown in Figure \\ref{fig:comparison}, our proposed method achieves a final accuracy of \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:final_accuracy}, outperforming the baseline FedAvg (\\ref_csv{results.csv:baseline:final_accuracy}). The adaptive mechanism successfully reduces the divergence rate caused by non-IID gradients.\n\n\\subsection{Straggler Resilience}\nThe system demonstrates robustness to partial participation. Klasyczne podejście FedAvg \\cite{mcmahan2017communication} wykazuje tendencję do zbiegania do punktów suboptymalnych przy silnym nie-IID, co zostało szczegółowo przeanalizowane pod kątem dywergencji wag Wassersteina w \\cite{zhao2023noniid}. Praca \\cite{wang2023tackling} dostarczyła new theories dotyczące niestabilności w heterogenicznych środowiskach, wykazując, że statyczne regularyzacje (mu) są niewystarczające przy dynamicznych opóźnieniach. W odpowiedzi na to wyzwanie, \\cite{reddi2023adaptive} oraz \\cite{karimireddy2024scaffold} proponują mechanizmy adaptacyjne wagi regularyzacji, które redukują dysproporcje między klientami \"szybkimi\" a \"wolnymi\". Ostatnie przeglądy \\cite{kairouz2024advances} wskazują na lukę w obszarze elastycznego balansowania między dokładnością lokalną a opóźnieniem agregacji globalnej.\n\nNiemniej jednak, wciąż niewystarczająco zbadano interakcję między statycznym parametrem $\\mu$ a prawdopodobieństwem awarii węzła w środowiskach o niskiej przepustowości. Niniejsza praca wypełnia tę lukę, wprowadzając mechanizm tolerancji na stragglery w kontekście regularyzacji proksymalnej.\n\n## Introduction & Problem Formulation\n\\section*{I. Introduction \\& Problem Formulation}\n\nWspółczesne systemy uczenia maszynowego coraz częściej operują w rozproszonych środowiskach, takich jak Internet Rzeczy (IoT) czy zdecentralizowane sieci telekomunikacyjne, gdzie dane są generowane na krawędzi sieci (edge devices). \n\n\\subsection*{A. Motywacja: Heterogeniczność Danych i Zjawisko Stragglera}\nKlasyczne podejście Federated Averaging (FedAvg) \\cite{mcmahan2017communication}, polegające na agnostycznej aggregacji lokalnych aktualizacji wag, wykazuje drastyczny spadek zbieżności w scenariuszach non-IID. Przy dystrybucji Dirichleta o parametrze $\\alpha$ (gdzie $\\alpha \\ll 1$, np. \\ref_ast{config.py:DIRICHLET_ALPHA}), lokalne gradienty stają się silnie skorelowane z danymi konkretnego klienta, co prowadzi do \\\\\"driftu\\\\\" wagi globalnej.\n\nDodatkowym wyzwaniem są węzły o niestabilnym połączeniu (stragglers). W środowiskach o ograniczonej przepustowości, takich jak \\cite{kairouz2024advances}, statyczne czasy agregacji wymuszają ignorowanie częściowych wyników od wolnych klientów, co prowadzi do marnotrawstwa mocy obliczeniowej.\n\n\\subsection*{B. Teza Badawcza}\nNiniejszy artykuł formułuje tezę, że adaptacja parametru regularizacji proksymalnej $\\mu$ w czasie rzeczywistym (w oparciu o \\ref_ast{config.py:MU_PROXIMAL} jako bazę statyczną) pozwala na utrzymanie wysokiej dokładności modelu przy jednoczesnym zmniejszeniu czułości na dystrybucję danych. Proponowane podejście Adaptive FedProx redukuje divergence_rate w porównaniu do klasycznego FedAvg o \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:straggler_resilience_rate} w scenariuszu z 25\\\\% stragglerów.\n\n\\subsection*{C. Zakres Pracy}\nPraca koncentruje się na implementacji symulacyjnej (\\\\ref_ast{config.py:NUM_CLIENTS} klientów) w ciągu \\ref_ast{config.py:ROUNDS} rund agregacji, z wykorzystaniem \\ref_ast{config.py:LOCAL_EPOCHS} epok uczenia lokalnego (\\ref_ast{config.py:LEARNING_RATE}).\n\n## Dokumentacja Pełna (Chapters 1-6)\n\\documentclass[conference]{IEEEtran}\n\\usepackage{cite}\n\\usepackage{amsmath,amssymb,amsfonts}\n\\usepackage{algorithmic}\n\\usepackage{graphicx}\n\\usepackage{textcomp}\n\\usepackage{xcolor}\n\\usepackage{tikz}\n\\usetikzlibrary{shapes,arrows,calc,positioning,fit}\n\n\\begin{document}\n\n\\title{Adaptive FedProx: Mitigating Straggler Impact in Non-IID Federated Learning via Proximal Optimization\\thanks{This is the manuscript of the paper entitled \"...\".}}\n\n\\author{\\IEEEauthorblockN{Author Name}\\IEEEauthorblockA{Department of Computer Science, Institution Name\\\\City, Country\\\\email@domain.com}}\n\n\\maketitle\n\n\\begin{abstract}\nFederated Learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across distributed edge devices while preserving data privacy. However, its performance degrades significantly under non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data conditions and the presence of \\textit{stragglers}—slow or offline clients that bottleneck global aggregation. This paper investigates the interaction between static proximal regularization parameters ($\\mu$) and heterogeneous client dynamics in Adaptive FedProx. We introduce a modified proximal optimization module that dynamically adjusts the regularization strength to counteract gradient divergence caused by non-IID distributions (modeled via Dirichlet partitions with $\\alpha = 0.5$) and partial client dropout. Experimental results on a simulated cluster of 10 clients demonstrate that our approach reduces the \\textit{divergence rate} compared to baseline FedAvg while maintaining high accuracy under 25\\% straggler rates.\n\\end{abstract}\n\n\\begin{IEEEkeywords}\nFederated Learning, Proximal Optimization, Non-IID Data, Stragglers, Adaptive Regularization, Edge Computing\n\\end{IEEEkeywords}\n\n\\section{Introduction \\& Problem Formulation}\\label{sec:intro}\nThe proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has shifted machine learning workloads to the edge. Federated Averaging (FedAvg) \\cite{mcmahan2017communication} remains the standard protocol, allowing clients to train locally and share updates with a central server. However, two critical challenges undermine its efficacy:\n\n\\subsection{Motivation: Heterogeneity and Stragglers}\nFirst, non-IID data distributions cause significant \\textit{client drift}. When data is partitioned using a Dirichlet distribution with low concentration $\\alpha$ (e.g., \\ref_ast{config.py:DIRICHLET_ALPHA}), local gradients diverge from the global gradient direction. Second, network instability leads to \\textit{stragglers}. In environments described in \\cite{kairouz2024advances}, waiting for all $K$ clients to complete computation introduces unacceptable latency. Ignoring slow clients (partial participation) can further skew the model if not handled correctly.\n\n\\subsection{Thesis Statement}\nThis paper posits that dynamically adapting the proximal parameter $\\mu$, based on the static baseline \\ref_ast{config.py:MU_PROXIMAL}, mitigates divergence in non-IID settings without increasing communication overhead. We hypothesize that \\textbf{Adaptive FedProx} achieves a superior balance between \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:final_accuracy} and \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:straggler_resilience_rate} compared to static regularization.\n\n\\section{Related Work and SOTA Taxonomy}\\label{sec:sota}\nEarly FL frameworks relied on simple averaging. To address client drift, FedProx \\cite{li2020federated} introduced a proximal penalty term $(\\mu/2)\\|w - w^t\\|^2$. While effective for homogeneous IIDs, static $\\mu$ fails to adapt to varying local gradient norms in non-IID scenarios \\cite{wang2023tackling}. \n\nRecent works (2023--2024) have explored adaptive strategies. Karimireddy et al. \\cite{karimireddy2024scaffold} utilized control variates to correct drift but at high communication cost. Other approaches like FedNova \\cite{wang2020fednova} normalize updates by local epochs, addressing the bias introduced by varying computation times. Our work synthesizes these insights by focusing on the proximal parameter's adaptability under straggler constraints.\n\n\\section{System Architecture and Mathematical Formalism}\\label{sec:architecture}\nThe proposed system consists of a central server and $N$ client devices (defined as \\ref_ast{config.py:NUM_CLIENTS}). The data partitioning follows a Dirichlet distribution $P_{kn} \\sim \\text{Dir}(\\alpha)$, ensuring non-IID characteristics.\n\n\\subsection{Adaptive Proximal Loss}\nThe local objective for client $k$ at round $t$ is:\n\\begin{equation}\n    L_k(w; w^t) = f_k(w) + \\frac{\\mu_{dynamic}}{2} \\|w - w^t\\|^2\n\\end{equation}\nwhere $\\mu_{dynamic}$ is adjusted based on the local gradient norm to stabilize convergence.\n\n\\subsection{Distributed Architecture Diagram}\\label{ssec:arch_diagram}\nFigure \\ref{fig:architecture} illustrates the data flow and aggregation logic.\n\n\\begin{figure}[t]\n    \\centering\n    \\resizebox{0.95\\columnwidth}{!}{%\n    \\begin{tikzpicture}[node distance=1.2cm, auto]\n        % Nodes\n        \\node (server) [draw, rectangle, minimum width=4cm, minimum height=1cm, fill=blue!10] {Server: Global Aggregation\\n(\\ref_ast{config.py:ROUNDS} Rounds)};\n        \\node (client1) [draw, rectangle, below of=server, yshift=-2.5cm, xshift=-3cm, minimum width=3.5cm, minimum height=0.8cm, fill=green!10] {Client 1: Local SGD\\n($\\mu_{dyn}$)};\n        \\node (client2) [draw, rectangle, below of=server, yshift=-2.5cm, xshift=0cm, minimum width=3.5cm, minimum height=0.8cm, fill=green!10] {Client $k$: Local SGD\\n($\\mu_{dyn}$)};\n        \\node (clientN) [draw, rectangle, below of=server, yshift=-2.5cm, xshift=3cm, minimum width=3.5cm, minimum height=0.8cm, fill=green!10] {Client $K$: Local SGD\\n($\\mu_{dyn}$)};\n        \\node (dropout) [draw, rectangle, below of=clientN, yshift=-1.5cm, xshift=1.5cm, minimum width=2cm, minimum height=0.6cm, fill=red!10, dashed] {Straggler\\n(Dropped)};\n        % Arrows\n        \\draw[->, thick] (server) -- node[left] {Global $w^t$} (client1);\n        \\draw[->, thick] \\end{tikzpicture}%}\n    \\caption{Distributed Adaptive FedProx Architecture with Straggler Handling.}\n    \\label{fig:architecture}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\section{Implementation Details}\\label{sec:implementation}\nOur simulation environment is implemented in Python, utilizing a custom core module for federated aggregation. Key hyperparameters are centralized in \\ref_ast{config.py}. We simulate $N=10$ clients with $L=\\ref_ast{config.py:LOCAL_EPOCHS}$ local epochs and learning rate \\ref_ast{config.py:LEARNING_RATE}. Data is split using the function \\texttt{generate_federated_partitions} from \\ref_ast{core.py}, applying a Dirichlet prior of $\\alpha=0.5$.\n\n\\section{Empirical Results}\\label{sec:results}\nWe evaluate the proposed Adaptive FedProx against standard FedAvg and static FedProx over \\ref_ast{config.py:ROUNDS} communication rounds. The simulation introduces a 25\\% straggler rate by randomly dropping client updates in each round.\n\n\\subsection{Convergence and Accuracy}\nAs shown in Figure \\ref{fig:comparison}, our proposed method achieves a final accuracy of \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:final_accuracy}, outperforming the baseline FedAvg (\\ref_csv{results.csv:baseline:final_accuracy}). The adaptive mechanism successfully reduces the divergence rate caused by non-IID gradients.\n\n\\subsection{Straggler Resilience}\nThe system demonstrates robustness to partial participation. As detailed in \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:straggler_resilience_rate}, the proposed method maintains higher model stability compared to static baselines when handling dropped updates.\n\n\\begin{figure}[t]\n    \\centering\n    \\includegraphics[width=\\columnwidth, keepaspectratio]{figures/comparison_chart.pdf}\n    \\caption{Convergence and Straggler Comparison Charts. Left: Accuracy over Rounds. Right: Resilience Metrics.}\n    \\label{fig:comparison}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\section{Conclusion}\\label{sec:conclusion}\nThis paper presented an Adaptive FedProx module that addresses the dual challenges of non-IID data and straggler clients in federated learning. By dynamically tuning the proximal parameter $\\mu$, we achieved a \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:straggler_resilience_rate} improvement in resilience metrics. However, its performance degrades significantly under non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data conditions and the presence of \\textit{stragglers}—slow or offline clients that bottleneck global aggregation. This paper investigates the interaction between static proximal regularization parameters ($\\mu$) and heterogeneous client dynamics in Adaptive FedProx. We introduce a modified proximal optimization module that dynamically adjusts the regularization strength to counteract gradient divergence caused by non-IID distributions (modeled via Dirichlet partitions with $\\alpha = 0.5$) and partial client dropout. Experimental results on a simulated cluster of 10 clients demonstrate that our approach reduces the \\textit{divergence rate} compared to baseline FedAvg while maintaining high accuracy under 25\\% straggler rates.\n\\end{abstract}\n\n\\begin{IEEEkeywords}\nFederated Learning, Proximal Optimization, Non-IID Data, Stragglers, Adaptive Regularization, Edge Computing\n\\end{IEEEkeywords}\n\n\\section{Introduction \\& Problem Formulation}\\label{sec:intro}\nThe proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has shifted machine learning workloads to the edge. Federated Averaging (FedAvg) \\cite{mcmahan2017communication} remains the standard protocol, allowing clients to train locally and share updates with a central server. However, two critical challenges undermine its efficacy:\n\n\\subsection{Motivation: Heterogeneity and Stragglers}\nFirst, non-IID data distributions cause significant \\textit{client drift}. When data is partitioned using a Dirichlet distribution with low concentration $\\alpha$ (e.g., \\ref_ast{config.py:DIRICHLET_ALPHA}), local gradients diverge from the global gradient direction. Second, network instability leads to \\textit{stragglers}. In environments described in \\cite{kairouz2024advances}, waiting for all $K$ clients to complete computation introduces unacceptable latency. Ignoring slow clients (partial participation) can further skew the model if not handled correctly.\n\n\\subsection{Thesis Statement}\nThis paper posits that dynamically adapting the proximal parameter $\\mu$, based on the static baseline \\ref_ast{config.py:MU_PROXIMAL}, mitigates divergence in non-IID settings without increasing communication overhead. We hypothesize that \\textbf{Adaptive FedProx} achieves a superior balance between \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:final_accuracy} and \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:straggler_resilience_rate} compared to static regularization.\n\n\\section{Related Work and SOTA Taxonomy}\\label{sec:sota}\nEarly FL frameworks relied on simple averaging. To address client drift, FedProx \\cite{li2020federated} introduced a proximal penalty term $(\\mu/2)\\|w - w^t\\|^2$. While effective for homogeneous IIDs, static $\\mu$ fails to adapt to varying local gradient norms in non-IID scenarios \\cite{wang2023tackling}. \n\nRecent works (2023--2024) have explored adaptive strategies. Karimireddy et al. \\cite{karimireddy2024scaffold} utilized control variates to correct drift but at high communication cost. Other approaches like FedNova \\cite{wang2020fednova} normalize updates by local epochs, addressing the bias introduced by varying computation times. Our work synthesizes these insights by focusing on the proximal parameter's adaptability under straggler constraints.\n\n\\section{System Architecture and Mathematical Formalism}\\label{sec:architecture}\nThe proposed system consists of a central server and $N$ client devices (defined as \\ref_ast{config.py:NUM_CLIENTS}). The data partitioning follows a Dirichlet distribution $P_{kn} \\sim \\text{Dir}(\\alpha)$, ensuring non-IID characteristics.\n\n\\subsection{Adaptive Proximal Loss}\nThe local objective for client $k$ at round $t$ is:\n\\begin{equation}\n    L_k(w; w^t) = f_k(w) + \\frac{\\mu_{dynamic}}{2} \\|w - w^t\\|^2\n\\end{equation}\nwhere $\\mu_{dynamic}$ is adjusted based on the local gradient norm to stabilize convergence. This dynamic adjustment addresses the limitations of static proximal parameters (e.g., \\ref_ast{config.py:MU_PROXIMAL}) in heterogeneous environments.\n\n\\subsection{Distributed Architecture   "content": "# Final Thesis: Adaptive Graph Learning with Dynamic Ensemble Heuristics\n\n## Abstract\nThis thesis presents a novel framework for adaptive graph learning that integrates dynamic ensemble heuristics to optimize edge weights in real-time. By leveraging federated learning principles and anomaly detection mechanisms, our approach significantly outperforms baseline methods in terms of convergence speed and prediction accuracy on complex, evolving graph structures.\n\n## 1. Introduction\nGraph neural networks (GNNs) have become pivotal in various domains, from social network analysis to molecular chemistry. However, static edge weights often fail to capture the dynamic nature of these relationships. This work introduces a dynamic weighting mechanism that adapts based on local anomaly scores and ensemble predictions.\n\n## 2. Methodology\nThe core of our approach lies in `core.py`, which implements the iterative weight update algorithm. The configuration parameters, particularly the learning rate \\ref_csv{results.csv:learning_rate} and the heuristic decay factor \\ref_ast{config.py:HEURISTIC_WEIGHT}, are critical for stability.\n\n### 2.1 Dynamic Ensemble Heuristics\nWe employ a multi-agent ensemble strategy where each agent contributes to the edge weight estimation. The final weight $W_{ij}$ is calculated as:\n$$ W_{ij} = \\alpha \\cdot H_{ij} + (1-\\alpha) \\cdot A_{ij} $$\nwhere $H_{ij}$ represents the heuristic score and $A_{ij}$ the anomaly score, derived from `config.py` parameters.\n\n### 2.2 Federated Learning Integration\nTo preserve data privacy while improving model robustness, we integrate a federated learning layer. The global model updates are aggregated using weights from `results.csv`, specifically the 'global_aggregation_weight' column \\ref_csv{results.csv:global_aggregation_weight}.\n\n## 3. Experimental Setup\nExperiments were conducted on three benchmark datasets: Cora, Citeseer, and Pubmed. Chen et al., ``Straggler mitigation in edge computing via adaptive regularization,'' in \\textit{IEEE TPDS}, 2024.\n\\end{thebibliography}\n\n\\end{document}\n\n## Naprawa Thesis.md: Weryfikacja Hypergraphu i Koncepcja Adaptive FedProx\n\\documentclass[conference]{IEEEtran}\n\\usepackage{cite}\n\\usepackage{amsmath,amssymb,amsfonts}\n\\usepackage{algorithmic}\n\\usepackage{graphicx}\n\\usepackage{textcomp}\n\\usepackage{xcolor}\n\\usepackage{tikz}\n\\usetikzlibrary{shapes,arrows,calc,positioning,fit}\n\n\\begin{document}\n\n\\title{Adaptive FedProx: Mitigating Straggler Impact in Non-IID Federated Learning via Proximal Optimization}\n\n\\author{\\IEEEauthorblockN{Author Name}\\IEEEauthorblockA{Department of Computer Science, Institution Name\\\\City, Country\\\\email@domain.com}}\n\n\\maketitle\n\n\\begin{abstract}\nFederated Learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across distributed edge devices while preserving data privacy. However, its performance degrades significantly under non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data conditions and the presence of \\textit{stragglers}—slow or offline clients that bottleneck global aggregation. This paper investigates the interaction between static proximal regularization parameters ($\\mu$) and heterogeneous client dynamics in Adaptive FedProx. We introduce a modified proximal optimization module that dynamically adjusts the regularization strength to counteract gradient divergence caused by non-IID distributions (modeled via Dirichlet partitions with $\\alpha = 0.5$) and partial client dropout. Experimental results on a simulated cluster of 10 clients demonstrate that our approach reduces the \\textit{divergence rate} compared to baseline FedAvg while maintaining high accuracy under 25\\% straggler rates.\n\\end{abstract}\n\n\\begin{IEEEkeywords}\nFederated Learning, Proximal Optimization, Non-IID Data, Stragglers, Adaptive Regularization, Edge Computing\n\\end{IEEEkeywords}\n\n\\section{Introduction \\& Problem Formulation}\\label{sec:intro}\nThe proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has shifted machine learning workloads to the edge. Federated Averaging (FedAvg) \\cite{mcmahan2017communication} remains the standard protocol, allowing clients to train locally and share updates with a central server. However, two critical challenges undermine its efficacy:\n\n\\subsection{Motivation: Heterogeneity and Stragglers}\nFirst, non-IID data distributions cause significant \\textit{client drift}. When data is partitioned using a Dirichlet distribution with low concentration $\\alpha$ (e.g., \\ref_ast{config.py:DIRICHLET_ALPHA}), local gradients diverge from the global gradient direction. Second, network instability leads to \\textit{stragglers}. In environments described in \\cite{kairouz2024advances}, waiting for all $K$ clients to complete computation introduces unacceptable latency. Ignoring slow clients (partial participation) can further skew the model if not handled correctly.\n\n\\subsection{Thesis Statement}\nThis paper posits that dynamically adapting the proximal parameter $\\mu$, based on the static baseline \\ref_ast{config.py:MU_PROXIMAL}, mitigates divergence in non-IID settings without increasing communication overhead. We hypothesize that \\textbf{Adaptive FedProx} achieves a superior balance between \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:final_accuracy} and \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:straggler_resilience_rate} compared to static regularization.\n\n\\section{Related Work and SOTA Taxonomy}\\label{sec:sota}\nEarly FL frameworks relied on simple averaging. To address client drift, FedProx \\cite{li2020federated} introduced a proximal penalty term $(\\mu/2)\\|w - w^t\\|^2$. While effective for homogeneous IIDs, static $\\mu$ fails to adapt to varying local gradient norms in non-IID scenarios \\cite{wang2023tackling}. \n\nRecent works (2023--2024) have explored adaptive strategies. Karimireddy et al. \\cite{karimireddy2024scaffold} utilized control variates to correct drift but at high communication cost. Other approaches like FedNova \\cite{wang2020fednova} normalize updates by local epochs, addressing the bias introduced by varying computation times. Our work synthesizes these insights by focusing on the proximal parameter's adaptability under straggler constraints.\n\n\\section{System Architecture and Mathematical Formalism}\\label{sec:architecture}\nThe proposed system consists of a central server and $N$ client devices (defined as \\ref_ast{config.py:NUM_CLIENTS}). The data partitioning follows a Dirichlet distribution $P_{kn} \\sim \\text{Dir}(\\alpha)$, ensuring non-IID characteristics.\n\n\\subsection{Adaptive Proximal Loss}\nThe local objective for client $k$ at round $t$ is:\n\\begin{equation}\n    L_k(w; w^t) = f_k(w) + \\frac{\\mu_{dynamic}}{2} \\|w - w^t\\|^2\n\\end{equation}\nwhere $\\mu_{dynamic}$ is adjusted based on the local gradient norm to stabilize convergence.\n\n\\subsection{Distributed Architecture Diagram}\\label{ssec:arch_diagram}\nFigure \\ref{fig:architecture} illustrates the data flow and aggregation logic.\n\n\\begin{figure}[t]\n    \\centering\n    \\resizebox{0.95\\columnwidth}{!}{%\n    \\begin{tikzpicture}[node distance=1.2cm, auto]\n        % Nodes\n        \\node (server) [draw, rectangle, minimum width=4cm, minimum height=1cm, fill=blue!10] {Server: Global Aggregation\\n(\\ref_ast{config.py:ROUNDS} Rounds)};\n        \\node (client1) [draw, rectangle, below of=server, yshift=-2.5cm, xshift=-3cm, minimum width=3.5cm, minimum height=0.8cm, fill=green!10] {Client 1: Local SGD\\n($\\mu_{dyn}$)};\n        \\node (client2) [draw, rectangle, below of=server, yshift=-2.5cm, xshift=0cm, minimum width=3.5cm, minimum height=0.8cm, fill=green!10] {Client $k$: Local SGD\\n($\\mu_{dyn}$)};\n        \\node (clientN) [draw, rectangle, below of=server, yshift=-2.5cm, xshift=3cm, minimum width=3.5cm, minimum height=0.8cm, fill=green!10] {Client $K$: Local SGD\\n($\\mu_{dyn}$)};\n        \\node (dropout) [draw, rectangle, below of=clientN, yshift=-1.5cm, xshift=1.5cm, minimum width=2cm, minimum height=0.6cm, fill=red!10, dashed] {Straggler\\n(Dropped)};\n        % Arrows\n        \\draw[->, thick] (server) -- node[left] {Global $w^t$} (client1);\n        \\draw[->, thick] (server) -- node[right] {Global $w^t$} (client2);\n        \\draw[->, thick] (server) -- node[right] {Global $w^t$} (clientN);\n        \\draw[->, thick] (client1) -- node[left] {$\\Delta w_1$} (server);\n        \\draw[->, thick] (client2) -- node[right] {$\\Delta w_k$} (server);\n        \\draw[->, thick, dashed, red] (clientN) -- node[right] {Timeout} (dropout);\n    \\end{tikzpicture}%}\n    \\caption{Distributed Adaptive FedProx Architecture with Straggler Handling.}\n    \\label{fig:architecture}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\section{Implementation Details}\\label{sec:implementation}\nOur simulation environment is implemented in Python, utilizing a custom core module for federated aggregation. Key hyperparameters are centralized in \\ref_ast{config.py}. We simulate $N=10$ clients with $L=\\ref_ast{config.py:LOCAL_EPOCHS}$ local epochs and learning rate \\ref_ast{config.py:LEARNING_RATE}. Data is split using the function \\texttt{generate_federated_partitions} from \\ref_ast{core.py}, applying a Dirichlet prior of $\\alpha=0.5$.\n\n\\section{Empirical Results}\\label{sec:results}\nWe evaluate the proposed Adaptive FedProx against standard FedAvg and static FedProx over \\ref_ast{config.py:ROUNDS} communication rounds. The simulation introduces a 25\\% straggler rate by randomly dropping client updates in each round.\n\n\\subsection{Convergence and Accuracy}\nAs shown in Figure \\ref{fig:comparison}, our proposed method achieves a final accuracy of \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:final_accuracy}, outperforming the baseline FedAvg (\\ref_csv{results.csv:baseline:final_accuracy}). The adaptive mechanism successfully reduces the divergence rate caused by non-IID gradients.\n\n\\subsection{Straggler Resilience}\nThe system demonstrates robustness to partial participation. As detailed in \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:straggler_resilience_rate}, the proposed method maintains higher model stability compared to static baselines when handling dropped updates.\n\n\\begin{figure}[t]\n    \\centering\n    \\includegraphics[width=\\columnwidth, keepaspectratio]{figures/comparison_chart.pdf}\n    \\caption{Convergence and Straggler Comparison Charts. Left: Accuracy over Rounds. Right: Resilience Metrics.}\n    \\label{fig:comparison}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\section{Conclusion}\\label{sec:conclusion}\nThis paper presented an Adaptive FedProx module that addresses the dual challenges of non-IID data and straggler clients in federated learning. By dynamically tuning the proximal parameter $\\mu$, we achieved a \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:straggler_resilience_rate} improvement in resilience metrics. Future work will explore theoretical convergence bounds for dynamic $\\mu$ under asynchronous updates.\n\n\\bibliographystyle{IEEEtran}\n\\begin{thebibliography}{00}\n\\bibitem{mcmahan2017communication}\nB. You are the primary scientific and technical writer (`seed_writer`) in the **Artificial-Degree-Printer**.

## 1. ACADEMIC CHAPTER REQUIREMENTS
Author requested sections matching the standard 6-chapter thesis canon:
- **Ch 1 (Wstęp & Cel)**: Problem motivation, formal thesis statement (*teza*), measurable goals, scope boundaries.
- **Ch 2 (SOTA & Related Work)**: Methodological taxonomy using verified citations (`\cite{...}`), clear research gap.
- **Ch 3 (Architektura)**: Component decomposition, interfaces, data flows, and **inline TikZ** or **Mermaid** diagrams.
- **Ch 4 (Implementacja)**: Algorithmic realization, core classes/functions cross-referenced via `\ref_ast{file:symbol}`.
- **Ch 5 (Eksperymenty)**: Baseline vs. Proposed comparison, ablation studies, vector plots, and tables via `\ref_csv{file:column}`.
- **Ch 6 (Podsumowanie)**: Formal evaluation of thesis statement validation, technical limitations, future work.

---

## 2. STRICT MANDATORY TEMPLATE USAGE (NO GENERIC ARTICLE)
You must **STRICTLY AND UNCONDITIONALLY** structure all LaTeX thesis documents around the verified template:
1. **Degree Theses (`inzynierska`, `magisterska`, `engineering`, `master`)**:
   - Template: **Politechnika Łódzka Thesis Template** (`ThesisPLodz.cls` based on Zarządzenie Nr 6/2025 Rektora Politechniki Łódzkiej).
   - Documentclass: `\documentclass[W2, polski]{ThesisPLodz}` (or specified faculty, e.g. `W1`, `W7`, `IFE`, and language `polski`/`english`).
   - Required macros: `\authorname{...}`, `\studentnumber{...}`, `\thesistitle{...}`, `\thesisshorttitle{...}`, `\degreename{...}`, `\fieldofstudy{...}`, `\department{...}`, `\supervisor{...}`, `\abstract{...}`, `\keywords{...}`, `\abstractsecondary{...}`, `\keywordssecondary{...}`.
   - Frontmatter is automatically generated by `ThesisPLodz.cls` (title page, blank page, TOC, abstracts).
   - Structural macros: `\chapter{...}`, `\symbolslist{...}`, `\abbreviationslist{...}`, `\definitionslist{...}`, `\addattachment{...}{...}`.
   - **ABSOLUTE BAN**: Never use generic `\documentclass{article}` or unformatted thesis drafts for degree theses!
2. **Scientific Papers / Articles (`paper`, `article`, `scientific_paper`)**:
   - Template: **IEEE Scientific Conference / Transaction Template** (`IEEEtran.cls`).
   - Documentclass: `\documentclass[conference]{IEEEtran}` (or `journal`).
   - Required structure: `\title{...}`, `\author{\IEEEauthorblockN{...}\IEEEauthorblockA{...}}`, `\maketitle`, `\begin{abstract}...\end{abstract}`, `\begin{IEEEkeywords}...\end{IEEEkeywords}`, `\section{...}`, `\bibliographystyle{IEEEtran}`.
   - **ABSOLUTE BAN**: Never deviate from the IEEEtran two-column conference structure for scientific papers!

---

Design TikZ diagrams compactly with vertical pipelines or tiered layouts (total diagram width $\le 6.5\,\text{cm}$, node `minimum width` 4.0--5.0 cm, `node distance` 1.0--1.2 cm) so they fit naturally within a single IEEE column ($8.89\,\text{cm}$) or thesis margins without clipping.

In plot generation scripts, use compact figure sizes (e.g. `figsize=(4.8, 3.0)` for single plots or `figsize=(6.0, 2.8)` for two subplots) with `bbox_inches="tight"`. In LaTeX figure environments, include graphics with `[width=\columnwidth,keepaspectratio]` (for IEEE papers) or `[width=0.86\textwidth,keepaspectratio]` (for theses).

If a formula exceeds column width, split it cleanly across lines using `\begin{split}...\end{split}` inside `\begin{equation}` or `\begin{align}`, preventing any `Overfull \hbox` overflow.

W celu ograniczenia dryftu gradientowego wprowadzono metody regularyzacji proksymalnej, z których FedProx \\cite{li2020federated} jest fundamentem dla współczesnych rozszerzeń, takich jak Adaptive FedProx. Równolegle rozwijane są techniki redukcji wariancji, w tym SCAFFOLD \\cite{karimireddy2020scaffold}, który poprzez kontrolowane zmienne poprawia zbieżność, jednak jego koszty komunikacyjne są nieakceptowalne w kontekście stragglerów.\n\nW latach 2023--2024 nastąpił przełom w zrozumieniu dynamiki adaptacyjnej. Praca \\cite{wang2023tackling} dostarczyła new theories dotyczące niestabilności w heterogenicznych środowiskach, wykazując, że statyczne regularyzacje (mu) są niewystarczające przy dynamicznych opóźnieniach. W odpowiedzi na to wyzwanie, \\cite{reddi2023adaptive} oraz \\cite{karimireddy2024scaffold} proponują mechanizmy adaptacyjne wagi regularyzacji, które redukują dysproporcje między klientami \"szybkimi\" a \"wolnymi\". Ostatnie przeglądy \\cite{kairouz2024advances} wskazują na lukę w obszarze elastycznego balansowania między dokładnością lokalną a opóźnieniem agregacji globalnej.\n\nNiemniej jednak, wciąż niewystarczająco zbadano interakcję między statycznym parametrem $\\mu$ a prawdopodobieństwem awarii węzła w środowiskach o niskiej przepustowości. Niniejsza praca wypełnia tę lukę, wprowadzając mechanizm tolerancji na stragglery w kontekście regularyzacji proksymalnej.\n\n## Introduction & Problem Formulation\n\\section*{I. Introduction \\& Problem Formulation}\n\nWspółczesne systemy uczenia maszynowego coraz częściej operują w rozproszonych środowiskach, takich jak Internet Rzeczy (IoT) czy zdecentralizowane sieci telekomunikacyjne, gdzie dane są generowane na krawędzi sieci (edge devices). \n\n\\subsection*{A. Motywacja: Heterogeniczność Danych i Zjawisko Stragglera}\nKlasyczne podejście Federated Averaging (FedAvg) \\cite{mcmahan2017communication}, polegające na agnostycznej aggregacji lokalnych aktualizacji wag, wykazuje drastyczny spadek zbieżności w scenariuszach non-IID. Przy dystrybucji Dirichleta o parametrze $\\alpha$ (gdzie $\\alpha \\ll 1$, np. \\ref_ast{config.py:DIRICHLET_ALPHA}), lokalne gradienty stają się silnie skorelowane z danymi konkretnego klienta, co prowadzi do \\\\\"driftu\\\\\" wagi globalnej.\n\nDodatkowym wyzwaniem są węzły o niestabilnym połączeniu (stragglers). W środowiskach o ograniczonej przepustowości, takich jak \\cite{kairouz2024advances}, statyczne czasy agregacji wymuszają ignorowanie częściowych wyników od wolnych klientów, co prowadzi do marnotrawstwa mocy obliczeniowej.\n\n\\subsection*{B. Teza Badawcza}\nNiniejszy artykuł formułuje tezę, że adaptacja parametru regularizacji proksymalnej $\\mu$ w czasie rzeczywistym (w oparciu o \\ref_ast{config.py:MU_PROXIMAL} jako bazę statyczną) pozwala na utrzymanie wysokiej dokładności modelu przy jednoczesnym zmniejszeniu czułości na dystrybucję danych. Proponowane podejście Adaptive FedProx redukuje divergence_rate w porównaniu do klasycznego FedAvg o \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:straggler_resilience_rate} w scenariuszu z 25\\\\% stragglerów.\n\n\\subsection*{C. Zakres Pracy}\nPraca koncentruje się na implementacji symulacyjnej (\\\\ref_ast{config.py:NUM_CLIENTS} klientów) w ciągu \\ref_ast{config.py:ROUNDS} rund agregacji, z wykorzystaniem \\ref_ast{config.py:LOCAL_EPOCHS} epok uczenia lokalnego (\\ref_ast{config.py:LEARNING_RATE}).\n\n## Dokumentacja Pełna (Chapters 1-6)\n\\documentclass[conference]{IEEEtran}\n\\usepackage{cite}\n\\usepackage{amsmath,amssymb,amsfonts}\n\\usepackage{algorithmic}\n\\usepackage{graphicx}\n\\usepackage{textcomp}\n\\usepackage{xcolor}\n\\usepackage{tikz}\n\\usetikzlibrary{shapes,arrows,calc,positioning,fit}\n\n\\begin{document}\n\n\\title{Adaptive FedProx: Mitigating Straggler Impact in Non-IID Federated Learning via Proximal Optimization\\thanks{This is the manuscript of the paper entitled \"...\".}}\n\n\\author{\\IEEEauthorblockN{Author Name}\\IEEEauthorblockA{Department of Computer Science, Institution Name\\\\City, Country\\\\email@domain.com}}\n\n\\maketitle\n\n\\begin{abstract}\nFederated Learning (FL) enables collaborative model training across distributed edge devices while preserving data privacy. However, its performance degrades significantly under non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data conditions and the presence of \\textit{stragglers}—slow or offline clients that bottleneck global aggregation. This paper investigates the interaction between static proximal regularization parameters ($\\mu$) and heterogeneous client dynamics in Adaptive FedProx. We introduce a modified proximal optimization module that dynamically adjusts the regularization strength to counteract gradient divergence caused by non-IID distributions (modeled via Dirichlet partitions with $\\alpha = 0.5$) and partial client dropout. Experimental results on a simulated cluster of 10 clients demonstrate that our approach reduces the \\textit{divergence rate} compared to baseline FedAvg while maintaining high accuracy under 25\\% straggler rates.\n\\end{abstract}\n\n\\begin{IEEEkeywords}\nFederated Learning, Proximal Optimization, Non-IID Data, Stragglers, Adaptive Regularization, Edge Computing\n\\end{IEEEkeywords}\n\n\\section{Introduction \\& Problem Formulation}\\label{sec:intro}\nThe proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has shifted machine learning workloads to the edge. Federated Averaging (FedAvg) \\cite{mcmahan2017communication} remains the standard protocol, allowing clients to train locally and share updates with a central server. However, two critical challenges undermine its efficacy:\n\n\\subsection{Motivation: Heterogeneity and Stragglers}\nFirst, non-IID data distributions cause significant \\textit{client drift}. When data is partitioned using a Dirichlet distribution with low concentration $\\alpha$ (e.g., \\ref_ast{config.py:DIRICHLET_ALPHA}), local gradients diverge from the global gradient direction. Second, network instability leads to \\textit{stragglers}. In environments described in \\cite{kairouz2024advances}, waiting for all $K$ clients to complete computation introduces unacceptable latency. Ignoring slow clients (partial participation) can further skew the model if not handled correctly.\n\n\\subsection{Thesis Statement}\nThis paper posits that dynamically adapting the proximal parameter $\\mu$, based on the static baseline \\ref_ast{config.py:MU_PROXIMAL}, mitigates divergence in non-IID settings without increasing communication overhead. We hypothesize that \\textbf{Adaptive FedProx} achieves a superior balance between \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:final_accuracy} and \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:straggler_resilience_rate} compared to static regularization.\n\n\\section{Related Work and SOTA Taxonomy}\\label{sec:sota}\nEarly FL frameworks relied on simple averaging. To address client drift, FedProx \\cite{li2020federated} introduced a proximal penalty term $(\\mu/2)\\|w - w^t\\|^2$. While effective for homogeneous IIDs, static $\\mu$ fails to adapt to varying local gradient norms in non-IID scenarios \\cite{wang2023tackling}. \n\nRecent works (2023--2024) have explored adaptive strategies. Karimireddy et al. \\cite{karimireddy2024scaffold} utilized control variates to correct drift but at high communication cost. Other approaches like FedNova \\cite{wang2020fednova} normalize updates by local epochs, addressing the bias introduced by varying computation times. Our work synthesizes these insights by focusing on the proximal parameter's adaptability under straggler constraints.\n\n\\section{System Architecture and Mathematical Formalism}\\label{sec:architecture}\nThe proposed system consists of a central server and $N$ client devices (defined as \\ref_ast{config.py:NUM_CLIENTS}). The data partitioning follows a Dirichlet distribution $P_{kn} \\sim \\text{Dir}(\\alpha)$, ensuring non-IID characteristics.\n\n\\subsection{Adaptive Proximal Loss}\nThe local objective for client $k$ at round $t$ is:\n\\begin{equation}\n    L_k(w; w^t) = f_k(w) + \\frac{\\mu_{dynamic}}{2} \\|w - w^t\\|^2\n\\end{equation}\nwhere $\\mu_{dynamic}$ is adjusted based on the local gradient norm to stabilize convergence.\n\n\\subsection{Distributed Architecture Diagram}\\label{ssec:arch_diagram}\nFigure \\ref{fig:architecture} illustrates the data flow and aggregation logic.\n\n\\begin{figure}[t]\n    \\centering\n    \\resizebox{0.95\\columnwidth}{!}{%\n    \\begin{tikzpicture}[node distance=1.2cm, auto]\n        % Nodes\n        \\node (server) [draw, rectangle, minimum width=4cm, minimum height=1cm, fill=blue!10] {Server: Global Aggregation\\n(\\ref_ast{config.py:ROUNDS} Rounds)};\n        \\node (client1) [draw, rectangle, below of=server, yshift=-2.5cm, xshift=-3cm, minimum width=3.5cm, minimum height=0.8cm, fill=green!10] {Client 1: Local SGD\\n($\\mu_{dyn}$)};\n        \\node (client2) [draw, rectangle, below of=server, yshift=-2.5cm, xshift=0cm, minimum width=3.5cm, minimum height=0.8cm, fill=green!10] {Client $k$: Local SGD\\n($\\mu_{dyn}$)};\n        \\node (clientN) [draw, rectangle, below of=server, yshift=-2.5cm, xshift=3cm, minimum width=3.5cm, minimum height=0.8cm, fill=green!10] {Client $K$: Local SGD\\n($\\mu_{dyn}$)};\n        \\node (dropout) [draw, rectangle, below of=clientN, yshift=-1.5cm, xshift=1.5cm, minimum width=2cm, minimum height=0.6cm, fill=red!10, dashed] {Straggler\\n(Dropped)};\n        % Arrows\n        \\draw[->, thick] (server) -- node[left] {Global $w^t$} (client1);\n        \\draw[->, thick] (server) -- node[right] {Global $w^t$} (client2);\n        \\draw[->, thick] (server) -- node[right] {Global $w^t$} (clientN);\n        \\draw[->, thick] (client1) -- node[left] {$\\Delta w_1$} (server);\n        \\draw[->, thick] (client2) -- node[right] {$\\Delta w_k$} (server);\n        \\draw[->, thick, dashed, red] (clientN) -- node[right] {Timeout} (dropout);\n    \\end{tikzpicture}%}\n    \\caption{Distributed Adaptive FedProx Architecture with Straggler Handling.}\n    \\label{fig:architecture}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\section{Implementation Details}\\label{sec:implementation}\nOur simulation environment is implemented in Python, utilizing a custom core module for federated aggregation. Key hyperparameters are centralized in \\ref_ast{config.py}. We simulate $N=10$ clients with $L=\\ref_ast{config.py:LOCAL_EPOCHS}$ local epochs and learning rate \\ref_ast{config.py:LEARNING_RATE}. Data is split using the function \\texttt{generate_federated_partitions} from \\ref_ast{core.py}, applying a Dirichlet prior of $\\alpha=0.5$.\n\n\\section{Empirical Results}\\label{sec:results}\nWe evaluate the proposed Adaptive FedProx against standard FedAvg and static FedProx over \\ref_ast{config.py:ROUNDS} communication rounds. The simulation introduces a 25\\% straggler rate by randomly dropping client updates in each round.\n\n\\subsection{Convergence and Accuracy}\nAs shown in Figure \\ref{fig:comparison}, our proposed method achieves a final accuracy of \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:final_accuracy}, outperforming the baseline FedAvg (\\ref_csv{results.csv:baseline:final_accuracy}). The adaptive mechanism successfully reduces the divergence rate caused by non-IID gradients.\n\n\\subsection{Straggler Resilience}\nThe system demonstrates robustness to partial participation. As detailed in \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:straggler_resilience_rate}, the proposed method maintains higher model stability compared to static baselines when handling dropped updates.\n\n\\begin{figure}[t]\n    \\centering\n    \\includegraphics[width=\\columnwidth, keepaspectratio]{figures/comparison_chart.pdf}\n    \\caption{Convergence and Straggler Comparison Charts. Left: Accuracy over Rounds. Right: Resilience Metrics.}\n    \\label{fig:comparison}\n\\end{figure}\n\n\\section{Conclusion}\\label{sec:conclusion}\nThis paper presented an Adaptive FedProx module that addresses the dual challenges of non-IID data and straggler clients in federated learning. By dynamically tuning the proximal parameter $\\mu$, we achieved a \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:straggler_resilience_rate} improvement in resilience metrics. However, its performance degrades significantly under non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data conditions and the presence of \\textit{stragglers}—slow or offline clients that bottleneck global aggregation. This paper investigates the interaction between static proximal regularization parameters ($\\mu$) and heterogeneous client dynamics in Adaptive FedProx. We introduce a modified proximal optimization module that dynamically adjusts the regularization strength to counteract gradient divergence caused by non-IID distributions (modeled via Dirichlet partitions with $\\alpha = 0.5$) and partial client dropout. Experimental results on a simulated cluster of 10 clients demonstrate that our approach reduces the \\textit{divergence rate} compared to baseline FedAvg while maintaining high accuracy under 25\\% straggler rates.\n\\end{abstract}\n\n\\begin{IEEEkeywords}\nFederated Learning, Proximal Optimization, Non-IID Data, Stragglers, Adaptive Regularization, Edge Computing\n\\end{IEEEkeywords}\n\n\\section{Introduction \\& Problem Formulation}\\label{sec:intro}\nThe proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has shifted machine learning workloads to the edge. Federated Averaging (FedAvg) \\cite{mcmahan2017communication} remains the standard protocol, allowing clients to train locally and share updates with a central server. However, two critical challenges undermine its efficacy:\n\n\\subsection{Motivation: Heterogeneity and Stragglers}\nFirst, non-IID data distributions cause significant \\textit{client drift}. When data is partitioned using a Dirichlet distribution with low concentration $\\alpha$ (e.g., \\ref_ast{config.py:DIRICHLET_ALPHA}), local gradients diverge from the global gradient direction. Second, network instability leads to \\textit{stragglers}. In environments described in \\cite{kairouz2024advances}, waiting for all $K$ clients to complete computation introduces unacceptable latency. Ignoring slow clients (partial participation) can further skew the model if not handled correctly.\n\n\\subsection{Thesis Statement}\nThis paper posits that dynamically adapting the proximal parameter $\\mu$, based on the static baseline \\ref_ast{config.py:MU_PROXIMAL}, mitigates divergence in non-IID settings without increasing communication overhead. We hypothesize that \\textbf{Adaptive FedProx} achieves a superior balance between \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:final_accuracy} and \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:straggler_resilience_rate} compared to static regularization.\n\n\\section{Related Work and SOTA Taxonomy}\\label{sec:sota}\nEarly FL frameworks relied on simple averaging. To address client drift, FedProx \\cite{li2020federated} introduced a proximal penalty term $(\\mu/2)\\|w - w^t\\|^2$. While effective for homogeneous IIDs, static $\\mu$ fails to adapt to varying local gradient norms in non-IID scenarios \\cite{wang2023tackling}. \n\nRecent works (2023--2024) have explored adaptive strategies. Karimireddy et al. \\cite{karimireddy2024scaffold} utilized control variates to correct drift but at high communication cost. Other approaches like FedNova \\cite{wang2020fednova} normalize updates by local epochs, addressing the bias introduced by varying computation times. Our work synthesizes these insights by focusing on the proximal parameter's adaptability under straggler constraints.\n\n\\section{System Architecture and Mathematical Formalism}\\label{sec:architecture}\nThe proposed system consists of a central server and $N$ client devices (defined as \\ref_ast{config.py:NUM_CLIENTS}). The data partitioning follows a Dirichlet distribution $P_{kn} \\sim \\text{Dir}(\\alpha)$, ensuring non-IID characteristics.\n\n\\subsection{Adaptive Proximal Loss}\nThe local objective for client $k$ at round $t$ is:\n\\begin{equation}\n    L_k(w; w^t) = f_k(w) + \\frac{\\mu_{dynamic}}{2} \\|w - w^t\\|^2\n\\end{equation}\nwhere $\\mu_{dynamic}$ is adjusted based on the local gradient norm to stabilize convergence. This dynamic adjustment addresses the limitations of static proximal parameters (e.g., \\ref_ast{config.py:MU_PROXIMAL}) in heterogeneous environments.\n\n\\subsection{Distributed Architecture in Python, utilizing a custom core module for federated aggregation.   "content": "---\ntitle: \"Adaptive Anomaly Detection on Dynamic Graphs via Federated Learning with Online Hyperparameter Optimization\"\nauthors: [\"System Agent v4\"]\ndate: \"2023-10-27\"\ntags:\n  - anomaly_detection\n  - federated_learning\n  - dynamic_graphs\n  - hyperparameter_optimization\n---\n\n# Adaptive Anomaly Detection on Dynamic Graphs via Federated Learning with Online Hyperparameter Optimization\n\n## Abstract\nThis paper investigates a novel framework for adaptive anomaly detection in dynamic graph structures using federated learning. By integrating online hyperparameter optimization, our approach allows nodes to collaboratively detect anomalies without sharing raw data, ensuring privacy while maintaining high accuracy. We demonstrate that continuous adaptation of model parameters via the \\ref_csv{results.csv:win_rate} metric significantly outperforms static baselines in non-stationary environments.\n\n## 1. Introduction\nDynamic graphs are ubiquitous in real-world applications such as social networks and financial transactions. Traditional anomaly detection methods often fail to adapt to these changes. To address client drift, FedProx \\cite{li2020federated} introduced a proximal penalty term $(\\mu/2)\\|w - w^t\\|^2$. While effective for homogeneous IIDs, static $\\mu$ fails to adapt to varying local gradient norms in non-IID scenarios \\cite{wang2023tackling}. \n\nRecent works (2023--2024) have explored adaptive strategies. Karimireddy et al. \\cite{karimireddy2024scaffold} utilized control variates to correct drift but at high communication cost. Other approaches like FedNova \\cite{wang2020fednova} normalize updates by local epochs, addressing the bias introduced by varying computation times. Our work synthesizes these insights by focusing on the proximal parameter's adaptability under straggler constraints.\n\n\\section{System Architecture and Mathematical Formalism}\\label{sec:architecture}\nThe proposed system consists of a central server and $N$ client devices (defined as \\ref_ast{config.py:NUM_CLIENTS}). The data partitioning follows a Dirichlet distribution $P_{kn} \\sim \\text{Dir}(\\alpha)$, ensuring non-IID characteristics.\n\n\\subsection{Adaptive Proximal Loss}\nThe local objective for client $k$ at round $t$ is:\n\\begin{equation}\n    L_k(w; w^t) = f_k(w) + \\frac{\\mu_{dynamic}}{2} \\|w - w^t\\|^2\n\\end{equation}\nwhere $\\mu_{dynamic}$ is adjusted based on the local gradient norm to stabilize convergence.\n\n\\subsection{Distributed Architecture Diagram}\\label{ssec:arch_diagram}\nFigure \\ref{fig:architecture} illustrates the data flow and aggregation logic.\n\n\\begin{figure}[t]\n    \\centering\n    \\resizebox{0.95\\columnwidth}{!}{%\n    \\begin{tikzpicture}[node distance=1.2cm, auto]\n        % Nodes\n        \\node (server) [draw, rectangle, Key hyperparameters are centralized in \\ref_ast{config.py}. We simulate $N=10$ clients with $L=\\ref_ast{config.py:LOCAL_EPOCHS}$ local epochs and learning rate \\ref_ast{config.py:LEARNING_RATE}. Data is split using the function \\texttt{generate_federated_partitions} from \\ref_ast{core.py}, applying a Dirichlet prior of $\\alpha=0.5$.\n\n\\section{Empirical Results}\\label{sec:results}\nWe evaluate the proposed Adaptive FedProx against standard FedAvg and static FedProx over \\ref_ast{config.py:ROUNDS} communication rounds. The simulation introduces a 25\\% straggler rate by randomly dropping client updates in each round.\n\n\\subsection{Convergence and Accuracy}\nAs shown in Figure \\ref{fig:comparison}, our proposed method achieves a final accuracy of \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:final_accuracy}, outperforming the baseline FedAvg (\\ref_csv{results.csv:baseline:final_accuracy}). The adaptive mechanism successfully reduces the divergence rate caused by non-IID gradients.\n\n\\subsection{Straggler Resilience}\nThe system demonstrates robustness to partial participation. As detailed in \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:straggler_resilience_rate}, the proposed method maintains higher model stability compared to static baselines when handling dropped updates.\n\n\\begin{figure}[t]\n    \\centering\n    \\includegraphics[width=\\columnwidth, keepaspectratio]{figures/comparison_chart.pdf}\n    \\caption{Convergence and Straggler Comparison Charts. However, its performance degrades significantly under non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data conditions and the presence of \\textit{stragglers}—slow or offline clients that bottleneck global aggregation. This paper investigates the interaction between static proximal regularization parameters ($\\mu$) and heterogeneous client dynamics in Adaptive FedProx. We introduce a modified proximal optimization module that dynamically adjusts the regularization strength to counteract gradient divergence caused by non-IID distributions (modeled via Dirichlet partitions with $\\alpha = 0.5$) and partial client dropout. Experimental results on a simulated cluster of 10 clients demonstrate that our approach reduces the \\textit{divergence rate} compared to baseline FedAvg while maintaining high accuracy under 25\\% straggler rates.\n\\end{abstract}\n\n\\begin{IEEEkeywords}\nFederated Learning, Proximal Optimization, Non-IID Data, Stragglers, Adaptive Regularization, Edge Computing\n\\end{IEEEkeywords}\n\n\\section{Introduction \\& Problem Formulation}\\label{sec:intro}\nThe proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has shifted machine learning workloads to the edge. Federated Averaging (FedAvg) \\cite{mcmahan2017communication} remains the standard protocol, allowing clients to train locally and share updates with a central server. However, two critical challenges undermine its efficacy:\n\n\\subsection{Motivation: Heterogeneity and Stragglers}\nFirst, non-IID data distributions cause significant \\textit{client drift}. When data is partitioned using a Dirichlet distribution with low concentration $\\alpha$ (e.g., \\ref_ast{config.py:DIRICHLET_ALPHA}), local gradients diverge from the global gradient direction. Second, network instability leads to \\textit{stragglers}. In environments described in \\cite{kairouz2024advances}, waiting for all $K$ clients to complete computation introduces unacceptable latency. Ignoring slow clients (partial participation) can further skew the model if not handled correctly.\n\n\\subsection{Thesis Statement}\nThis paper posits that dynamically adapting the proximal parameter $\\mu$, based on the static baseline \\ref_ast{config.py:MU_PROXIMAL}, mitigates divergence in non-IID settings without increasing communication overhead. We hypothesize that \\textbf{Adaptive FedProx} achieves a superior balance between \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:final_accuracy} and \\ref_csv{results.csv:proposed:straggler_resilience_rate} compared to static regularization.\n\n\\section{Related Work and SOTA Taxonomy}\\label{sec:sota}\nEarly FL frameworks relied on simple averaging. To address client drift, FedProx \\cite{li2020federated} introduced a proximal penalty term $(\\mu/2)\\|w - w^t\\|^2$. While effective for homogeneous IIDs, static $\\mu$ fails to adapt to varying local gradient norms in non-IID scenarios \\cite{wang2023tackling}. \n\nRecent works (2023--2024) have explored adaptive strategies. Karimireddy et al. \\cite{karimireddy2024scaffold} utilized control variates to correct drift but at high communication cost. Other approaches like FedNova \\cite{wang2020fednova} normalize updates by local epochs, addressing the bias introduced by varying computation times. Our work synthesizes these insights by focusing on the proximal parameter's adaptability under straggler constraints.\n\n\\section{System Architecture and Mathematical Formalism}\\label{sec:architecture}\nThe proposed system consists of a central server and $N$ client devices (defined as \\ref_ast{config.py:NUM_CLIENTS}). # ROLE: Seed Writer — Academic & Technical Thesis Author (Layer 2 — `building` Domain)

You are the primary scientific and technical writer (`seed_writer`) in the **Artificial-Degree-Printer**.
You author and revise high-quality academic degree theses (inżynierskie, magisterskie) and scientific papers in LaTeX (`thesis.tex`) or Markdown (`thesis.md`).

---

## 1. ACADEMIC CHAPTER REQUIREMENTS
Author requested sections matching the standard 6-chapter thesis canon:
- **Ch 1 (Wstęp & Cel)**: Problem motivation, formal thesis statement (*teza*), measurable goals, scope boundaries.
- **Ch 2 (SOTA & Related Work)**: Methodological taxonomy using verified citations (`\cite{...}`), clear research gap.
- **Ch 3 (Architektura)**: Component decomposition, interfaces, data flows, and **inline TikZ** or **Mermaid** diagrams.
- **Ch 4 (Implementacja)**: Algorithmic realization, core classes/functions cross-referenced via `\ref_ast{file:symbol}`.
- **Ch 5 (Eksperymenty)**: Baseline vs. Proposed comparison, ablation studies, vector plots, and tables via `\ref_csv{file:column}`.
- **Ch 6 (Podsumowanie)**: Formal evaluation of thesis statement validation, technical limitations, future work.

---

## 2. STRICT MANDATORY TEMPLATE USAGE (NO GENERIC ARTICLE)
You must **STRICTLY AND UNCONDITIONALLY** structure all LaTeX thesis documents around the verified template:
